cards.title: Optimal proof systems outside NP
cards.formal: Does there exist a nonempty language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) that has an optimal Cook–Reckhow proof system, where optimality compares proof lengths and does not require an efficient translation between systems?

cards.why: Determines whether a proof language can be best up to polynomial proof-length overhead even when membership has no uniformly short certificates. It separates optimality relative to all competing proof systems from the existence of short proofs themselves.

sentences: The question asks whether any language outside NP has an optimal proof system.
Each system is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps proofs to exactly the statements in its language.
Optimality means that every competing system’s proofs can be matched with at most polynomial growth in length.
A fast algorithm for translating proofs is a separate, stronger requirement.
Recent oracle barriers and jump-operator results do not decide the ordinary existence question.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. Such a language is automatically computably enumerable, because it is the range of \(f\); decidability is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional example of a language \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) and prove that it has an optimal system under the stated simulation relation, or prove that every language admitting such an optimal system belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). A conditional existence theorem, an oracle construction, or an example using advice or a weaker simulation relation does not by itself settle this question.

context_blocks.title: The easy existence boundary
context_blocks.text: Every nonempty language in \(\mathrm{NP}\) has an ordinary optimal proof system. This does not imply \(p\)-optimality. The source also reviews languages outside \(\mathrm{NP}\) for which optimal systems provably do not exist; these examples do not cover every language outside the class.

context_blocks.title: Oracle barriers leave the unrelativized question open
context_blocks.text: Egidy and Glaßer construct one oracle with no optimal systems for languages in \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), and another with no optimal systems for computably enumerable languages outside nondeterministic quasipolynomial time. The first also has an infinite polynomial hierarchy; the second has \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\). These are limitations on arguments that remain valid relative to arbitrary oracles, rather than a universal negative answer in the ordinary computational model.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 paper studies a separate constructive issue
context_blocks.text: A recursive jump operator would effectively turn each proof system for a language into one it cannot simulate. Its existence rules out an optimal system. The source investigates the converse relationship, while explicitly retaining the general existence question outside \(\mathrm{NP}\).

cards.context:
Every nonempty language in \(\mathrm{NP}\) has an ordinary optimal proof system. This does not imply \(p\)-optimality. The source also reviews languages outside \(\mathrm{NP}\) for which optimal systems provably do not exist; these examples do not cover every language outside the class.

Egidy and Glaßer construct one oracle with no optimal systems for languages in \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), and another with no optimal systems for computably enumerable languages outside nondeterministic quasipolynomial time. The first also has an infinite polynomial hierarchy; the second has \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\). These are limitations on arguments that remain valid relative to arbitrary oracles, rather than a universal negative answer in the ordinary computational model.

A recursive jump operator would effectively turn each proof system for a language into one it cannot simulate. Its existence rules out an optimal system. The source investigates the converse relationship, while explicitly retaining the general existence question outside \(\mathrm{NP}\).

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.
